title: Levin Mows with the Peasants
text:
In Anna Karenina, the landowner Konstantin Levin, restless and unhappy, decided one summer to go out and mow hay with the peasants on his own estate. He took a scythe and joined the line of mowers at dawn.

At first it went badly. He was out of practice, he swung too hard, and the rows he cut were ragged. An old peasant in the line showed him how to do it, and the young man behind him was pressing at his heels. Levin sweated and ached and was afraid he would have to give up in front of everyone. But he kept on, row after row, matching his pace to the man ahead.

Then something changed. As the day went on, there came moments when he stopped thinking about the scythe at all. It seemed to move by itself, and the whole line of men moved together in one rhythm. Those were the happiest moments. When he started thinking about what he was doing, the work grew hard again.

At midday he ate bread with the peasants and drank water from the stream. By evening they had mowed a large meadow that in the morning had looked impossible. Levin walked home tired and happier than he had been in a long time.
lesson: Hard work done in rhythm with others can become a source of joy. Learn from the people who already do it well, and match their pace before trying to set your own.
source: Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina, Part III, chapters 4 to 6
